32afa5384ddda64e.copy: How we build Off the clock How we build Notes from the projects on this page All Tally & Trace Central Command This site Our workflow 20 posts 19 Nov 2026 Redesigning Tally & Trace So It Stops Looking Generated An audit of why a working, accessible money app still looked like every other app made with an AI helper, the two directions we drew up, why we picked the green ledger pad, and how every change was measured in a browser instead of judged by eye. Tally & Trace 18 Nov 2026 Checking the Statement Against the App: Reconciliation in Tally & Trace How Tally & Trace reconciles a credit card statement without the server ever seeing the PDF: a small JSON document, a pure diff function, a fingerprinted apply that verifies itself, and the closing-day detour that a rehearsal on real-shaped data found. Tally & Trace 14 Nov 2026 Why Tally & Trace Felt Slow, and What We Did About It One dashboard endpoint grew from about 20 SQL statements to 530, on a free-tier instance with a tenth of a CPU. Here are the root causes, the fixes in the order they shipped, and the before and after numbers. Tally & Trace 6 Nov 2026 Teaching the Audit to Decide: Jev and Audit Autonomy, Phase A Three independent auditors on every plan and pull request caught real defects, but they also caused owner pauses and repeated full rounds. Phase A adds a policy file, an adjudicator in shadow, a narrow yes/no judge called Jev, and go-live rules based on data, so the system can show what is safe to automate before anything is. 5 Nov 2026 The Sheet Is the Oracle: Cutting Tally & Trace Over From the Spreadsheet How Tally & Trace finally replaced the Google Sheet it was built to retire: not by importing data, but by making the app reproduce the Sheet's balances and month-by-month projections, then proving it with a load that refuses to guess and a check that never trusts the load. Tally & Trace 2 Nov 2026 The Session's Word Never Counts: Trailhead's Workstation Dispatcher How Trailhead swapped its phase engine for one long-lived workstation running interactive Claude Code sessions, and how a deterministic dispatcher around it decides what ships: a go gate, a prompt queue, checks, blind audits and one verified tree, proven byte-identical to the frozen commit. 14 Oct 2026 From Entities to Owners: Reworking Tally & Trace How Tally & Trace's projection engine grew from a pooled balance into card statements, spending wallets and loans, why shared 'entities' were replaced by single-owner records, tags and Drive-style shared accounts, and how every audit finding was reproduced before it was fixed. Tally & Trace 23 Sep 2026 Three Auditors, No Shortcuts: The Triple Audit Why every plan and every pull request now gets three independent reviews from three different model families, how the auditors are kept blind to each other and to the writer, what that costs, and the rules that stop it turning into an endless review loop. 23 Sep 2026 Rewriting Trailhead: From Vanilla JS to Svelte 5 and Fastify Why Trailhead was rebuilt in a fresh repository instead of patched, how a ten-ticket migration was ordered around its critical path, and what three independent AI auditors found when they reviewed the brand-new web UI. 7 Sep 2026 A Tap on the Shoulder: Alerts, Urgent Tickets, and Push for Central Command Central Command could only help when its tab was open. Three features shipped together to change that: Linear, Slack, and Trello feeding the notifications spine, an urgency-scored tickets card, and an installable app that can send push notifications. Central Command 2 Sep 2026 Who Watches the Watchman? Connecting the Homelab to Central Command Our homelab monitors itself, but what happens when the monitor goes down with it? We built an external heartbeat to find out. Central Command 20 Jul 2026 Wiring Sentry Into a Finance App Without Leaking the Money Adding error and performance monitoring to Tally & Trace — off by default, PII scrubbed on both surfaces, and Session Replay deliberately left switched off. It's live and reporting, but there's no war story yet: the interesting part is the config, not the outcome. Tally & Trace 19 Jul 2026 Which Account Comes Up Short: Per-Account Solvency in Tally & Trace The cash-flow timeline used to pool every account into one balance. Now it routes each bill primary→overflow and tells you exactly which account can't cover what — plus credit-card statement modelling, hardened auth, and what's coming next. Tally & Trace 13 Jul 2026 The Month-End Total Lied: Modeling Cash-Flow Timing in Tally & Trace Our budget app faithfully computed a reassuring month-end total — and was blind to the mid-month moment where the bills come due before payday. Here's how we reworked the forecast engine to model the one number the spreadsheet actually existed to compute. Tally & Trace 13 Jun 2026 Carrying the Hardening Over: Security Pass on Central Command The same security goals as the portfolio pass — dependency hygiene, security headers, a CSP, and abuse protection on public endpoints — re-derived for a Cloudflare-native stack. Run a full marathon Finally finished our first full one and I couldn't be more proud of my wife for pushing through despite recovering from flu and battling severe cramps midway through. Honestly, I wanted to give up so many times during the race but I saw how determined you were to finally get this big win so I just sucked it up and tried to be as positive as I could. I knew how hard you trained for this and there was no way in hell I would let that go to waste. You deserve this!!! I might keep complaining but I will forever be your running buddy. Happy valentines day!

90ba6b1290a9c8e9.copy: A previous post rebuilt Tally & Trace's forecaster into a day-ordered running-balance engine — one that could finally see the mid-month trough where the bills come due before payday. It shipped with an honest limitation: it pooled every account into a single balance. That's the right first answer to "am I solvent this month," and the wrong answer to the question that actually clears a payment: can this account cover this bill, on the day it's due? This update closes that gap, and brings a few other pieces of the spreadsheet across with it. Shipped Per-account solvency, with payment routing The forecaster now projects a running balance per account, not one merged number. Each payable is routed the way we actually pay it: from a primary account first, and only the overflow from a designated second account. When the primary can't cover a bill, the engine draws the remainder from overflow — and if that still isn't enough before the due date, it flags the shortfall with the specific account, the amount short, and the date. "You're fine on paper but Card A is ₱X short on the 24th" is a sentence the old pooled view structurally couldn't say. Bill due (with due date) Primary account covers it? Yes Paid from primary No Cover the remainder from overflow account Overflow covers the rest before the due date? Yes Paid — split across accounts No Flag shortfall: which account, how much short, on what date How a bill is routed, primary first, then overflow. Credit-card statement modelling Credit cards no longer show up as a single lump. The engine derives one dated payable per billing cycle straight from the card's own transactions — walking each card's close day to its due date — and routes that statement payment to its funding account like any other bill. This also fixed a modelling bug: an unposted card charge used to leave cash on its purchase date, as if you paid at the register. A credit purchase doesn't touch cash until the statement is due, so the forecast now defers the cash impact to the payment date, where it belongs. Also shipped Installment "n of m" tracking — recurring installments now carry their position in the plan ("Payment 3 of 12", "9 left"), so a financed purchase reads as progress toward payoff instead of an anonymous recurring line. Auth & config hardening — refresh tokens are now rotating and revocable, moved out of XSS-readable localStorage into httpOnly cookies. A production config guard refuses to boot with a placeholder SECRET_KEY or DATABASE_URL, and datetimes are timezone-aware end to end. Multi-entity, for real — co-members of a business entity now see each other's records, while personal data stays owner-only. The isolation model finally works both ways: shared where it should be shared, private where it must stay private. A correctness baseline — a growing pytest suite pins the money math: balances, transfers with fees, allocations, and FX round-tripping, all at full Decimal precision. The properties are blunt on purpose, because a finance tool that's almost right isn't right. What's next The forecaster can now tell you which account comes up short before payday. The next step is letting you ask it — and act on what it says — without opening the app. We're designing an MCP connector that lets you read your finances, and make guarded changes, by talking to Claude: "what bills are due before payday?", "mark the electric bill paid." The plan is deliberately staged — read-only tools first, guarded writes second — everything entity-scoped and gated behind revocable personal-access tokens, so access is narrow, auditable, and easy to cut off. This is in design, not shipped; we'd rather get the guardrails right than rush the writes. Why this matters The throughline hasn't changed since day one: exact money math, and solvency before the bill hits. Every figure stays in Decimal from the database to the forecast — no floating-point drift in numbers that decide whether rent clears. What this update adds is precision about where the money is: not just "will the month net out," but "will this specific account cover this specific bill on the day it's due." That's the question a household actually asks at the end of the month — and now it's the one the app answers first.
